analysis.one_liner: Restores the right of student loan borrowers to wipe out their loans in bankruptcy.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Judiciary Committee without a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: Since 2005, federal law has made almost all student loans—government and private—nearly impossible to erase in bankruptcy, unlike credit card debt, medical bills, or a mortgage. This bill repeals that special exception, so student borrowers could discharge their loans like any other debt. It was introduced by Senator Durbin with 21 cosponsors and never moved after being referred to the Judiciary Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Current and former student borrowers who are in genuine financial distress would gain the same bankruptcy escape hatch that exists for nearly every other kind of debt, including a fresh start after job loss, illness, or disability.

how_it_helps.text: It strikes the bankruptcy code provision (11 U.S.C. § 523(a)(8)) that carves out student loans from discharge, letting borrowers erase nonprofit, government, or private student loans in bankruptcy like other unsecured debt.
It also lets borrowers discharge obligations to repay educational benefits, scholarships, or stipends.
The change applies only to bankruptcy cases filed after the date of enactment, so it would not reopen closed cases.

analysis.who_pays: Lenders—chiefly the federal government, which holds most student loans, plus private student lenders—and the loan servicers and collectors whose revenue depends on debts being repaid would bear more losses from defaulted loans. Future borrowers could face somewhat higher rates or tighter underwriting because lenders could no longer count on bankruptcy-proof debt.

drawbacks.text: Because lenders could no longer rely on loans being almost impossible to erase, the change would likely push private lenders to charge higher rates or screen borrowers more strictly, and could add costs to the federal loan program.

The bill makes the discharge rule permanent and unconditional—it contains no requirement to try income-based repayment first or to limit abuse, which critics of broad student-loan discharge have traditionally demanded.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For borrowers already in deep distress, the benefit is large and immediate—the same fresh start available on medical or credit card debt—while the cost falls on lenders and, indirectly, on future borrowers through somewhat higher pricing. The bill is written as a clean repeal of the exception without guardrails, so its actual effect on future borrowing costs would depend on how lenders and courts adapt.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate read it twice and sent it to the Judiciary Committee, which never held a hearing or vote on it, and the bill expired when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Durbin introduced the bill on May 9, 2019, joined by 21 cosponsors (20 Democrats and 1 independent).
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary.
No further action—no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote—appears in the action history through the end of the 116th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal and private student lenders, along with the servicers and collectors who profit from repayment, keep the special protection that makes student loans nearly impossible to erase in bankruptcy. Borrowers in financial distress remain stuck with debts almost everyone else can discharge.

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to restore student borrowers' bankruptcy rights.

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Signed on as an original cosponsor when the bill was introduced.

for.name: Sen. Bernie Sanders and 19 other cosponsors

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-SC)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never scheduled a hearing or markup, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 22 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats or independents; no Republican cosponsor appears on the bill, and the Republican-controlled Senate never acted on it.

industries.note: The federal Direct Loan program holds most student debt, and its special bankruptcy protection is what keeps defaults collectible for decades. Dischargeability would make defaults a real loss to the loan program, whose cost falls partly on taxpayers.
Private lenders since 2005 have enjoyed bankruptcy-proof debt, letting them lend at low risk. Losing that protection raises their losses on defaults and their cost of lending.

industries.industry: Student loan servicers and debt collectors
industries.note: These firms earn fees on collecting debts for decades after graduation. Wiping out unpayable loans in bankruptcy shrinks the pool of debt available to collect.
